Hi Gabrielle,

I change slightly the R Documentation from unmarked to answer your question. Using a simplest model (no covariates), you can use backTransform to get abundance (latent in your samples) and p.

Best,

José

#==========================

# Simulate data

set.seed(35)

nSites <- 100

nVisits <- 3

lambda <- 3                      # expected counts at each site

N <- rpois(nSites, lambda)       # latent abundance

y <- matrix(NA, nSites, nVisits)

p <- 0.3                         # fix detection prob for each visit

for(j in 1:nVisits) {

  y[,j] <- rbinom(nSites, N, p)

}

umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y=y, siteCovs=NULL, obsCovs=NULL)

summary(umf)

# Fit a model

fm1 <- pcount(~1 ~1, umf, K=50)

fm1

backTransform(fm1, type="state")    # lambda

backTransform(fm1, type="det")      # p

Dear all,

I am new to occupancy modelling so forgive me if it's a stupid question.
I have 124 sites monitored via camera traps. We consider each 24h (starting at midday to have the complete night) as secondary receptions, and we repeated the survey of each site during the wet and dray season.
We are not interested in colonisation and extinction as we consider our population closed between the 2 periods. But we want to use season as a covariate to explain detectability at each site.

Is it correct to simply the occu function and include season as an observation covariate (which will then only affect detection and not occupancy)?

Thanks!
Stephanie

messages.body_plain:
Fear ye not colext!

Yes, you could use occu but have season as a site covariate.  Something like:  occu(~ 1 ~ 0 + season, ufo)

However, I'd argue that because you do survey the same sites in both seasons and it would be good to have appropriate standard errors (accounting for that matching) to assess the assumption of equal detection probabilities across seasons, then colext would be a better choice.  And the added bonus is that the parameter estimates will be nearly identical.

Here's on of the colext examples in the documentation (just slightly modified to match your 124 sites and 2 seasons).  But first the results:

# From colext:  psi1 =  0.4663238  psi2 =  0.5728308
# From occu:    psi1 =  0.4664261  psi2 =  0.5730348

> # Generate some data with 124 sites
> M <- 124 # Number of sites
> J <- 3 # num secondary sample periods
> T <- 2 # num primary sample periods
> psi <- rep(NA, T) # Occupancy probability
> muZ <- z <- array(dim = c(M, T)) # Expected and realized occurrence
> y <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J, T)) # Detection histories
> set.seed(13973)
> psi[1] <- 0.4 # Initial occupancy probability
> p <- c(0.3,0.4,0.5,0.5,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.5,0.6,0.2)
> phi <- runif(n=T-1, min=0.6, max=0.8) # Survival probability (1-epsilon)
> gamma <- runif(n=T-1, min=0.1, max=0.2) # Colonization probability
> # Generate latent states of occurrence
> # First year
> z[,1] <- rbinom(M, 1, psi[1]) # Initial occupancy state
> # Later years
> for(i in 1:M){ # Loop over sites
> for(k in 2:T){ # Loop over years
> muZ[k] <- z[i, k-1]*phi[k-1] + (1-z[i, k-1])*gamma[k-1]
> z[i,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[k])
> }
> }
> # Generate detection/non-detection data
> for(i in 1:M){
> for(k in 1:T){
> prob <- z[i,k] * p[k]
> for(j in 1:J){
> y[i,j,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob)
> }
> }
> }

> # colext analysis
> yy <- matrix(y, M, J*T)
> year <- matrix(c('01','02'),
> nrow(yy), T, byrow=TRUE)
> simUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy,
>   yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year), numPrimary=T)
> fm = colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, simUMF)
> # Brute force transformation of parameter estimates
> psi1 = 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@estimates@estimates$psi@estimates))
> e = 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@estimates@estimates$ext@estimates))
> g = 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@estimates@estimates$col@estimates))
> psi2 = (1-psi1)*g + psi1*(1-e)
>
> # occu analysis
> y2 = rbind(y[,,1],y[,,2])
> site.covs2 = data.frame(season = c(rep("Season 1",M),rep("Season 2",M)))
> ufo = unmarkedFrameOccu(y = y2, siteCovs = site.covs2)
> fm2 = occu(~ 1 ~ 0 + season, ufo)
> psi = 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm2@estimates@estimates$state@estimates))
>
> # Summary
> cat("From colext:  psi1 = ",psi1, " psi2 = ",psi2,"\n")
> # From colext:  psi1 =  0.4663238  psi2 =  0.5728308
>
> cat("From occu: psi1 = ",psi[1], " psi2 = ",psi[2],"\n")
> # From occu: psi1 =  0.4664261  psi2 =  0.5730348

Dear Cody,

I would say that it does (a little). Not closure, but the assumption of independence of occupancy status among sites. But unless this is likely to happen often, I would not care too much: in the history of statistics and ecology  there has never been any assumption that is always totally met.

So the important thing usually is that an assumption is not violated too much or too often. Of course, this is a judgment call to some degree. Individuals moving among neighbouring sites will induce residual spatial autocorrelation in occupancy, i.e., a spatial pattern that cannot be explained by covariates. If you are worried about spatial autocorrelation in occupancy, you could fit an occupancy model with CAR prior e.g. in Win/OpenBUGS or use the R package stocc.

Best regards  --  Marc

Hi Cody,

OK, but in this case, you would have to move from likelihood inference (that's what Bob Dorazio presents, right ?) to Bayes, since to account for spatial autocorrelation you have to go down the MCMC avenue. Unless you are very interested in this, I would not do this right now perhaps, because you would have to translate the Dorazio model into BUGS.

Most ecological data analyses do not account for all likely sources of dependence in the data, absolutely most. So unless you have serious worries about such an "overlap" in the detection radii of your sites I would simply ignore this.

About spatio-temporal autocorrelation: of course, but while spatial autocorrelation is typically just a nuisance, temporal autocorrelation is not: it's population dynamics mostly that is responsible for the latter and this of course is very much at the center of interest of an ecological study. So best to parametrize temporal autocorrelation in a biological meaningful manner, i.e., with some population model.

Best regards  --- Marc

Yes, I don't think that colext allows such restrictions on the parameters such as wanting psi1 = psi2.

So writing the log likelihood and accounting for such restrictions is what one needs to do.  (A restriction such as p1 = p2 works fine in colext.)

If you have no missing values and both seasons have the same number of visits and the parameters are psi1, gamma, epsilon, p1, and p2, then one can simplify the likelihood function by calculating the "sufficient" statistics:  m1 (total nu​mber of detections in season 1), m2 (total number of detectins in season 2), n00 (total number of sites with no detections in both seasons), n01 (total number of sites with no detections in season 1 but detections in season 2), n10 (total number of sites with detections in seasons 1 but no detections in season 2), and n11 (total number of sites with detections in both seasons).

Below is some (brute force) code that will find the maximum likelihood estimates under various restrictions (some of which colext will also perform - and I've included the equivalent colext code for those cases).  I've also assumed in the code that the data is stored in an unmarkedMultFrame named simUMF (from the previous code) and the sufficient statistics are grabbed from there.

> # Log likelihood functions for various restrictions on parameters
> logL = function(z, v1, v2, n00, n01, n10, n11, m1, m2) {
>    # Parameters are psi1, g (colononizatin probability),
>    # e (extinction probability),
>    # p1 (detection probability for season 1)
>    # and p2 (detection probability for season 2)
>    psi1 = z[1]
>    g = z[2]
>    e = z[3]
>    p1 = z[4]
>    p2 = z[5]
>    n11*log((1 - e)*psi1) +
>    n01*log((1 - psi1)*g + psi1*(1 - e)*(1 - p1)^v1) +
>    n10*log(psi1*e + psi1*(1 - e)*(1 - p2)^v2) +
>    n00*log((1 - psi1)*(1 - g) + (1 - psi1)*g*(1 - p2)^v2 +
>      psi1*e*(1 - p1)^v1 + psi1*(1 - e)*(1-p1)^v1 * (1 - p2)^v2) +
>    m1*log(p1) + (v1*(n10+n11)-m1)*log(1-p1) +
>    m2*log(p2) + (v2*(n01+n11)-m2)*log(1-p2)
> }
>
> logL2 = function (z, v1, v2, n00, n01, n10, n11, m1, m2) {
>   # Restriction:  p1 = p2
>   psi1 = z[1]
>   g = z[2]
>   e = z[3]
>   p = z[4]
>   logL(c(psi1, g, e, p, p), v1, v2, n00, n01, n10, n11, m1, m2)
> }
>
> logL3 = function (z, v1, v2, n00, n01, n10, n11, m1, m2) {
>   # Restriction:  psi1 = psi2
>   psi1 = z[1]
>   e = z[2]

> >      psi1*e*(1 - p1)^v1 + psi1*(1 - e)*(1-p1)^v1 * (1 - p2)^v2) +
> >    m1*log(p1) + (v1*(n10+n11)-m1)*log(1-p1) +

To assess bias, you would need to simulate many datasets. Have you tried that?

Hi Mike, I am a biologist trying to publish a paper on otter habitat selection using functions occu and pcount.  My data consist of 4-7 back-to-back segments in a row up a total of 10 rivers, each segment being 450m long.  I have sub-divided each segment into 150m "sub-segments" (which have commonly been used in the literature as 3 separate "visit" within each 450 m segment (site)).  I have created 2 detection covariates (track substrates and scat substrates) and my response variable (total sign) at the 150m "sub-segents" and are using them as observation-level covariates, along with about a few habitat site-level covariates. Chris,

I looked at your script and I think you're close.  Bear in mind that a variogram isn't necessary to calculate the autocovariate.  I think it's fine to just calculate a series of autocovariate values based on different neighborhood distances, plug them into your model/s, and then settle on the distance that results in the lowest AIC.

I don't recommend using a neighborhood distance that encompasses different sites/blocks (rivers in your case).  Then your autocovariate values will be influenced by differences between sites and not by autocorrelation.  So if you have 4-7 segments in a river, each 450 m long, I wouldn't consider anything more than around 3200 m.

Here's some of your script I played with.  You could also justify trying the autocovariate as a detection variable.

library(spdep)
ac3200 <-autocov_dist(z=ab, xy=coord, nbs=3200, type="inverse",style="B",longlat=FALSE, zero.policy=TRUE)
siteCovsAC <- cbind(siteCovs,ac3200)
siteCovsAC[1,]

Best regards --  Marc

I am hoping that the 6 year gap doesn’t prevent us from running multi-season models, and if it does what would be a good alternative?".

Why would you expect a bias ? I don't see why the estimates from a model with long intervals lacking observations should be biased. Presumably, you will get pretty bad estimates, in terms of the precision, but this is exactly what you would like to have: that your model accounts for the added uncertainty induced by the lacking observations.

As so often, one could say "Simulation is the answer" :) If you are worried about the behaviour of the model in this specific situation, then why not run a simple simulation, say, with exactly your sample size (and missing value pattern) specifications and perhaps with all parameters (psi1, col, ext, p) varying randomly according to 4 uniform distributions over the range that you expect for your species ? Then, you fit the model to 100 simulated data sets and see how good the estimates become.

We have a function dynocc.fn in the AHMbook package, which simulates regular (i.e., balanced) dynocc data. You can then shoot missing values into the resulting data sets to create a data set that looks like yours in terms of the missing values.

hi Shelby,

OK, that makes sense to me. In Markov models such as the dynocc model, when you have missing occasions, I think the easiest is to "fill them up" in the data with NAs. Now, to be honest, I don't know whether colext will take that, but you ought to try. If not, you could use BUGS software, there such things are easy.

In a model without NA-filled-in data for missing primary occasions, there is nothing wrong with fitting a model with full time-dependence in the col-ext parameters: the params for the long intervals will simply have a different meaning from those associated wit the regular interval length. But problems start as soon as you want to constrain that fully time-dep model for instance by making the parameters constant or covariate dependent.

Best regards  --- Marc

Chris, if the spatial autocovariate alleviated spatial autocorrelation, then I think at a minimum it should be an important variable--models that contain it should have a lower AIC than models that don't.  So if this isn't happening, I'm not sure what's going on, except apparently the autocovariate isn't capturing the spatial autocorrelation.

Another option for you is to run a mixed model.  I believe you would use river as a random effect and the habitat variables you're interested in as fixed effects.  This should account for spatial autocorrelation/pseudoreplication within rivers.  The disadvantage is that mixed effect models are not run through unmarked (unless something has changed recently).  I understand that there's a way to combine a mixed effect model and an n-mixture model using Bayesian methods in WinBUGS, but I've never gone that route and so can't advise any further on that.

Mike
